cases.doctrine: A freeze order requires facts showing a probable connection between the specific account/property and unlawful activity; a broad list of accounts or income-versus-transactions inference is not enough where the evidentiary link is missing. The burden of proving probable cause always rests with the AMLC, never with the account owners (though the burden of evidence may shift once AMLC makes a prima facie case).
cases.examUse: For freeze orders, analyze probable cause and the specific property-to-activity link; AMLC bears the burden. Quote: the burden of proving probable cause always rests with the AMLC.
cases.facts: AMLC investigated alleged anomalous DBP loan accommodations to Deltaventure Resources, Inc., transactions involving DBP's Philex shares, and related transfers/sales, and sought to freeze many bank accounts as related to unlawful activity and money laundering. The CA lifted the freeze over most accounts, keeping only a Bank of Commerce account of Boerstar Corporation linked by evidence to the transactions.
cases.issue: Whether AMLC sufficiently established probable cause to keep the freeze orders over the unfrozen accounts, and whether the burden shifted to account holders to prove legitimacy.
cases.name: Republic v. Ongpin
cases.ruling: The Court denied the Republic's petition and affirmed lifting the freeze over all but the demonstrably linked account, stressing that freeze and bank-inquiry orders are extraordinary remedies.

sourceRefs.section: Case digest — Republic v. Ongpin, G.R. No. 207078 (June 20, 2022)

cases.doctrine: The Sec. 9(c) confidentiality/tipping-off rule does not automatically bar AMLC from participating in prosecutions or lawfully disclosing information in its investigative/prosecutorial functions. A CTR/STR as financial intelligence must be distinguished from bank records and evidence obtainable through lawful processes.
cases.examUse: Distinguish the covered person's tipping-off ban from AMLC's own investigative role: AMLC is not merely a repository of reports.
cases.facts: In a criminal case over second-hand helicopters represented as brand new, the prosecution sought AMLC records and testimony on covered/suspicious transaction reports for a bank account; AMLC invoked AMLA confidentiality against disclosure.
cases.issue: Whether AMLA Sec. 9(c) prohibited AMLC itself from disclosing covered or suspicious transaction reports in criminal proceedings.
cases.name: Republic v. Sandiganbayan and Office of the Ombudsman
cases.ruling: The Court rejected AMLC's blanket position: the Sec. 9(c) prohibition targets covered persons and their officers/employees to prevent tipping-off, while AMLC has separate statutory investigative and case-institution functions.

sourceRefs.section: Case digest — Republic v. Sandiganbayan and Office of the Ombudsman, G.R. Nos. 232724–27 (February 15, 2021)

cases.doctrine: Bank secrecy yields to express statutory exceptions. An ex parte AMLA bank inquiry is valid when court-authorized because advance notice could defeat the investigation by allowing funds or evidence to be moved — but it is not a general license for unrestricted access to all accounts.
cases.examUse: For bank inquiry, identify the legal authority and the bank-secrecy exception; explain the ex parte rationale and its statutory safeguards.
cases.facts: The Republic, through AMLC, sought authority to inquire into a bank account during an anti-money-laundering investigation; the account holder challenged the bank-inquiry mechanism and ex parte (no prior notice) authorization as unconstitutional and violative of deposit confidentiality and due process.
cases.issue: Whether the AMLA bank-inquiry provision and its ex parte procedure were unconstitutional or impermissibly intruded on confidentiality and due process.
cases.name: Republic v. Eugenio, Jr.
cases.ruling: The Court upheld the mechanism as an extraordinary provisional remedy aiding money-laundering investigation, reasoning that prior notice could frustrate the probe; the remedy must stay within statutory conditions and safeguards.

sourceRefs.section: Case digest — Republic v. Eugenio, Jr., G.R. No. 174629 (February 14, 2008)

cases.doctrine: The constitutional ban on imprisonment for debt does not invalidate B.P. Blg. 22 because the offense is the issuance of a worthless check — a public-welfare offense under the police power — rather than non-payment alone.
cases.examUse: State the debt-versus-worthless-check distinction and cite police power. Court's key wording: The gravamen of the offense punished by BP 22 is the act of making and issuing a worthless check.
cases.facts: Several BP 22 accused challenged the law as violating the ban on imprisonment for debt, impairing freedom of contract, denying equal protection, and suffering enactment defects.
cases.issue: Is B.P. Blg. 22 unconstitutional because it may impose imprisonment for a check connected with a debt?
cases.name: Lozano v. Martinez
cases.ruling: No. The Court upheld the law: it penalizes issuing and circulating worthless checks, which affects public confidence in checks and banking — a valid police-power measure.

cases.doctrine: An issuance falls outside B.P. Blg. 22 when the prosecution fails to establish the first element — that the check was issued to apply on account or for value. The exact transaction and evidence matter.
cases.examUse: Idos is evidence-specific, not a blanket guarantee-check exemption: the check merely evidenced a future partnership share with no present debt or account. Court's key wording: The check was not intended to apply on account or for value.
cases.facts: After dissolving their partnership, Idos issued postdated checks evidencing Alarilla's proportionate share, payable from future sale of goods and collection of receivables. One check was dishonored; Idos maintained it was assurance of an eventual share, not payment of a debt or existing account.
cases.issue: Was the check issued to apply on account or for value under Sec. 1 of B.P. Blg. 22?
cases.name: Idos v. Court of Appeals and People
cases.ruling: No. The record showed no present debt or account due and payable for the check; the Court also found insufficient proof of actual knowledge of insufficiency and no adequate proof of notice of dishonor. Acquitted.

sourceRefs.section: Case Digest: Idos v. Court of Appeals and People

cases.doctrine: A check issued as a guarantee or deposit is not for that reason alone outside B.P. Blg. 22; the purpose of issuance does not automatically create an exemption.
cases.examUse: Contrast with Idos: guarantee purpose alone never exempts, but the State must still prove every element. Court's key wording: Batas Pambansa Bilang 22 applies even in cases where dishonored checks are issued merely in the form of a deposit or a guarantee.
cases.facts: Victor Que, connected with Powerhouse Supply, Inc., argued his BP 22 checks merely guaranteed company purchases; the checks were dishonored and lower courts sustained conviction.
cases.issue: Does issuance merely as a guarantee or security remove a check from B.P. Blg. 22?
cases.name: Que v. People
cases.ruling: No. The law does not distinguish payment checks from guarantee checks; reconsideration denied, conviction stood.

cases.doctrine: A signatory is not automatically guilty because a signed check later bounces. Knowledge must be proved beyond reasonable doubt, and the Sec. 2 notice requirement must be satisfied before its presumption can apply.
cases.examUse: Test knowledge and notice separately: corporate role without treasury control plus no personal notice defeats the presumption. Court's key wording: The prosecution has a duty to prove all the elements of the crime, including the acts that give rise to the prima facie presumption.
cases.facts: Marketing employee Lina Lim Lao signed blank corporate checks as routine work; another person filled in payee and amounts. The checks bounced; she had no treasury/funding control, and the notice sent to the corporate main office was not shown personally received by her.
cases.issue: Can an employee be convicted without proof of actual knowledge of insufficiency or actual notice of dishonor?
cases.name: Lim Lao v. Court of Appeals and People
cases.ruling: No. Knowledge is essential, the presumption is only prima facie and rebuttable, and corporate notice was not personal notice to her. Acquitted.

sourceRefs.section: Case Digest: Lim Lao v. Court of Appeals and People

cases.doctrine: The prosecution must prove the evidentiary requirements for dishonor and the notice triggering the Sec. 2 presumption. Criminal acquittal does not erase the separate civil obligation to pay the debt the checks represent.
cases.examUse: Reading Secs. 2 and 3 together: written notice of dishonor plus the 5-banking-day opportunity is required. Court's key wording: Without the written notice of dishonor, there can be no basis for establishing the presence of actual knowledge of insufficiency of funds.
cases.facts: Evangeline Cabrera was convicted on three BP 22 counts for checks to Luis Go; on review she showed the demand letter was never formally offered and the evidence did not adequately prove actual written notice to her.
cases.issue: Could the convictions stand without adequate proof of written notice of dishonor and the statutory chance to pay or arrange payment?
cases.name: Cabrera v. People
cases.ruling: No. Convictions reversed and Cabrera acquitted for failure of proof beyond reasonable doubt; her civil obligation for the checks' face value was upheld.

cases.doctrine: B.P. Blg. 22 and estafa are separate offenses with different elements; no double jeopardy arises merely because the same act or check is involved, as long as each prosecution independently meets its legal requirements.
cases.examUse: Estafa needs deceit + damage; BP 22 does not. Sec. 5 preserves RPC liability. Court's key wording: A single criminal act may give rise to a multiplicity of offenses.
cases.facts: Peter Nierras bought oil products from Pilipinas Shell and issued nine checks on delivery; the account was closed and the checks bounced. He faced both BP 22 and Art. 315(2)(d) estafa cases and claimed the later estafa prosecutions were double jeopardy.
cases.issue: May a person be prosecuted under both B.P. Blg. 22 and Art. 315(2)(d) for the same bouncing checks?
cases.name: Nierras v. Dacuycuy
cases.ruling: Yes. The offenses are distinct; a single act may violate both laws when both element sets are satisfied, and Sec. 5 expressly preserves RPC liability. Petition dismissed (certiorari also held an improper remedy against denial of a motion to quash).

provisions.citation: RA 9160, Sec. 2, as amended by RA 11521
provisions.explanation: State policy to protect the integrity and confidentiality of bank accounts, keep the Philippines from being used as a money-laundering site, cooperate in transnational investigations/prosecutions, and implement targeted financial sanctions. Banking privacy and AMLA enforcement work together: privacy is not absolute when a lawful AMLA process applies.
provisions.verbatim: It is hereby declared the policy of the State to protect and preserve the integrity and confidentiality of bank accounts and to ensure that the Philippines shall not be used as a money laundering site for the proceeds of any unlawful activity. Consistent with its foreign policy, the State shall extend cooperation in transnational investigations and prosecutions of persons involved in money laundering activities wherever committed, as well as in the implementation of targeted financial sanctions related to the financing of the proliferation of weapons of mass destruction, terrorism, and financing of terrorism, pursuant to the resolution of the United Nations Security Council.

provisions.citation: RA 10365, Sec. 1 (amending AMLA Sec. 3(a)), read with RA 11521
provisions.explanation: Defines covered persons across BSP-, IC-, and SEC-supervised sectors plus designated businesses (jewelry, company service providers, client-asset managers). RA 11521 adds real estate developers/brokers and offshore gaming operators/service providers. Covered persons bear customer-identification, record-keeping, monitoring, and reporting duties.
provisions.verbatim: ‘Covered persons’, natural or juridical, refer to: (1) banks, non-banks, quasi-banks, trust entities, foreign exchange dealers, pawnshops, money changers, remittance and transfer companies and other similar entities and all other persons and their subsidiaries and affiliates supervised or regulated by the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP); (2) insurance companies, pre-need companies and all other persons supervised or regulated by the Insurance Commission (IC); (3) (i) securities dealers, brokers, salesmen, investment houses and other similar persons managing securities or rendering services as investment agent, advisor, or consultant, (ii) mutual funds, close-end investment companies, common trust funds, and other similar persons, and (iii) other entities administering or otherwise dealing in currency, commodities or financial derivatives based thereon, valuable objects, cash substitutes and other similar monetary instruments or property supervised or regulated by the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC); (4) jewelry dealers in precious metals, who, as a business, trade in precious metals, for transactions in excess of One million pesos (₱1,000,000.00); (5) jewelry dealers in precious stones, who, as a business, trade in precious stones, for transactions in excess of One million pesos (₱1,000,000.00); (6) company service providers which, as a business, provide services to third parties such as acting as a formation agent, director or corporate secretary, providing a registered office or business address, or acting as a nominee shareholder; and (7) persons who provide services such as managing client money, securities or other assets; managing bank, savings or securities accounts; organizing contributions for companies; or creating, operating or managing juridical persons or arrangements and buying or selling business entities.

provisions.explanation: Customer-identification duty: establish/record true identity on official documents, verify corporate clients' existence/structure/representatives, and never open anonymous or fictitious-name accounts (non-checking numbered accounts allowed). Restated by 2018 IRR Rule 18, Sec. 3.1 for all customers, agents, and legal arrangements.
provisions.verbatim: (a) Customer Identification. — Covered persons shall establish and record the true identity of their clients based on official documents. They shall maintain a system of verifying the true identity of their clients and, in case of corporate clients, require a system of verifying their legal existence and organizational structure, as well as the authority and identification of all persons purporting to act on their behalf. Anonymous accounts, accounts under fictitious names, and all other similar accounts shall be absolutely prohibited, subject to the statutory allowance for non-checking numbered accounts.

provisions.explanation: Record-keeping duty: keep all transaction records for 5 years from the transaction; for closed accounts, keep identification, account files, and correspondence for at least 5 years from closure, so fund movements can be reconstructed.
provisions.verbatim: All records of all transactions of covered persons shall be maintained and safely stored for five (5) years from the date of transactions. With respect to closed accounts, the records on customer identification, account files and business correspondence shall be preserved and safely stored for at least five (5) years from the dates when they were closed.

provisions.explanation: Reporting duty: report all covered and suspicious transactions within 5 working days (supervising authority may allow up to 10); dual-nature transactions are reported as suspicious. Good-faith reporters are immune from proceedings; covered persons/officers/employees must not tip off customers. The Sec. 9(c) confidentiality rule binds covered persons, not AMLC's own investigative disclosures (Republic v. Sandiganbayan).
provisions.verbatim:
Covered persons shall report to the AMLC all covered transactions and suspicious transactions within five (5) working days from occurrence thereof, unless the Supervising Authority prescribes a longer period not exceeding ten (10) working days. Should a transaction be determined to be both a covered transaction and a suspicious transaction, the covered person shall be required to report the same as a suspicious transaction.

However, no administrative, criminal or civil proceedings shall lie against any person for having made a covered or suspicious transaction report in the regular performance of his duties in good faith, whether or not such reporting results in any criminal prosecution under this Act or any other law.

provisions.explanation: Threshold-based reporting trigger: general cash/equivalent over ₱500,000 in one banking day; single casino cash over ₱5,000,000; single real-estate cash over ₱7,500,000; the IRR adds jewelry/precious-metal/stone dealer transactions over ₱1,000,000. Crossing the threshold triggers reporting, not criminal liability. The old ₱4M/five-days threshold is obsolete.
provisions.verbatim: ‘Covered transactions’ is a transaction in cash or other equivalent monetary instrument involving a total amount in excess of Five hundred thousand pesos (₱500,000.00) within one (1) banking day; for covered persons under Section 3(a)(8), a single casino cash transaction involving an amount in excess of Five million pesos (₱5,000,000.00) or its equivalent in any other currency. For covered persons under Section 3(a)(9) herein, a single cash transaction involving an amount in excess of Seven million five hundred thousand pesos (₱7,500,000.00) or its equivalent in any other currency.

provisions.explanation: Monetary instrument covers currency and financial instruments (coins/currency, drafts, checks, notes, securities and similar instruments through which title can pass). Person means any natural or juridical person. Proceeds means an amount derived or realized from an unlawful activity. Transaction means any act establishing a right/obligation or contractual/legal relationship, including any movement of funds by any means with a covered institution. (Reviewer presents these defined terms with gloss rather than a single continuous quotation; no verbatim field.)

Seven red flags with no minimum amount: no legal/trade purpose; unidentified client; amount incommensurate with capacity; structuring to evade reporting; deviation from client profile; link to unlawful activity; or similar/analogous transactions. An STR is financial intelligence for analysis, not proof of guilt.
provisions.verbatim: ‘Suspicious transactions’ are transactions with covered persons, regardless of the amounts involved, where any of the following circumstances exist: (1) There is no underlying legal or trade obligation, purpose or economic justification; (2) The client is not properly identified; (3) The amount involved is not commensurate with the business or financial capacity of the client; (4) Taking into account all known circumstances, it may be perceived that the client’s transaction is structured in order to avoid being the subject of reporting requirements under the Act; (5) Any circumstance relating to the transaction which is observed to deviate from the profile of the client and/or the client’s past transactions with the covered person; (6) The transaction is in any way related to an unlawful activity or offense under this Act that is about to be, is being or has been committed; or (7) Any transaction that is similar or analogous to any of the foregoing.

provisions.citation: 2018 AMLA IRR, Rule 2 and Rule 23 (Jan. 2021 amendment)
provisions.explanation: Beneficial owner = the natural person who ultimately owns/controls the customer or on whose behalf the transaction is done. The SEC builds the identification/record-keeping/publication mechanisms, requires accurate and regularly updated beneficial-ownership information, and ensures juridical persons cooperate with AMLC/supervising authorities, including through an authorized resident natural person.

sourceRefs.section: 5. Beneficial ownership (2018 AMLA IRR, Rules 23 and 24)

provisions.verbatim:
‘Beneficial Owner’ refers to any natural person who: (1) ultimately owns or controls the customer and/or on whose behalf a transaction or activity is being conducted.

The SEC is hereby enlisted to develop mechanisms that identify and describe the following: (a) Different types, forms and basic features of legal persons in the country; (b) Processes for the creation of those legal persons; and (c) Processes for obtaining and recording of basic and beneficial ownership information. The SEC shall develop a mechanism to make the information on the legal persons and their beneficial owners publicly available, as may be allowed under existing laws.

The SEC shall require companies and corporate clients, respectively, to submit accurate and regularly updated beneficial ownership information.

provisions.explanation: For legal arrangements, covered persons must require express-trust trustees to obtain and hold adequate, accurate, current identity information on trustors/grantors/settlors, the trustee, beneficiaries or class of beneficiaries, and any other natural person exercising ultimate effective control. (Only the quoted phrase below is an explicit quotation; the balance is the reviewer's paraphrase.)

sourceRefs.section: 5. Beneficial ownership (2018 AMLA IRR, Rules 23 and 24)

provisions.verbatim: adequate, accurate, and current information

provisions.explanation: Accounts only in the true and full name of the owner/holder; anonymous/fictitious/similar accounts absolutely prohibited; only non-checking numbered accounts allowed, and their CTRs/STRs must name the true holder; supervising authorities may test annually for such accounts. (Syllabus cites Rule 2, Sec. 1(1)(n), but that is the 'Beneficiary' definition in the amended IRR; Rule 17 is the operative rule.)
provisions.verbatim:
Section 1. Anonymous Accounts and Accounts under Fictitious Names. 1.1. Covered persons shall maintain customers’ account only in the true and full name of the account owner or holder. 1.2. Anonymous accounts, accounts under fictitious names, and all other similar accounts shall be absolutely prohibited.

Section 2. Numbered Accounts. 2.1. Numbered accounts, except non-checking numbered accounts, shall not be allowed. 2.2. CTRs and STRs involving non-checking numbered accounts shall contain the true name of the account holder.

Section 3. Annual Testing to Determine True Identity of Accounts. The SAs may conduct annual testing for the sole purpose of determining the existence and true identity of the foregoing accounts, if any.

provisions.explanation: CDD purposes (identify customer/agents/beneficial owners; assess risk; manage the relationship; calibrate monitoring), six CDD measures (identification, verification, agent checks, beneficial-ownership verification, purpose determination, ongoing monitoring), scrutiny of complex/unusual transactions with EDD for higher risk, and refusal/termination plus STR filing when CDD cannot be completed.
provisions.verbatim:
Covered persons shall conduct CDD for the following purposes: (a) To identify the customer, and its agents and beneficial owners; (b) To determine the risk posed by each customer; (c) To establish, maintain, close or terminate the account or business relationship; and (d) To assess the level of monitoring to be applied.

Covered persons shall conduct the appropriate CDD measures, which include the following procedures: (a) Customer Identification Process; (b) Customer Verification Process; (c) Identification and Verification of Agents; (d) Beneficial Ownership Verification; (e) Determination of the Purpose of Relationship; and (f) Ongoing Monitoring Process.

Covered persons shall identify and record the true identity of their customers, whether permanent or occasional, and whether natural or juridical person, or legal arrangement.

Covered persons shall examine the background and purpose of all complex, unusually large transactions, all unusual patterns of transactions, which have no apparent economic or lawful purpose, and other transactions that may be considered suspicious. Where the risks are higher, covered persons shall conduct EDD.

provisions.explanation: Six modes of committing money laundering with knowledge that the instrument/property represents, involves, or relates to proceeds of unlawful activity: transact; convert/transfer/dispose/move/acquire/possess/use; conceal/disguise; attempt/conspire; aid/abet/assist/counsel; or facilitate by act or omission. Knowledge and the proceeds link must be established.
provisions.verbatim: Money laundering is committed by any person who, knowing that any monetary instrument or property represents, involves, or relates to the proceeds of any unlawful activity: (a) transacts said monetary instrument or property; (b) converts, transfers, disposes of, moves, acquires, possesses or uses said monetary instrument or property; (c) conceals or disguises the true nature, source, location, disposition, movement or ownership of or rights with respect to said monetary instrument or property; (d) attempts or conspires to commit money laundering offenses referred to in paragraphs (a), (b) or (c); (e) aids, abets, assists in or counsels the commission of the money laundering offenses referred to in paragraphs (a), (b) or (c) above; and (f) performs or fails to perform any act as a result of which he facilitates the offense of money laundering referred to in paragraphs (a), (b) or (c) above.

provisions.explanation: Lists predicate/unlawful activities whose proceeds may be laundered: kidnapping for ransom; drugs; graft/plunder; robbery/extortion; illegal gambling; piracy; qualified theft; swindling; smuggling; e-commerce/securities offenses; hijacking; terrorism/terrorism financing; bribery/corruption; public-funds frauds; forgery/counterfeiting; trafficking; forestry/fisheries/mining/wildlife/caves offenses; carnapping; illegal firearms/explosives; fencing; migrant-worker offenses; IP offenses; voyeurism; child-protection offenses; strategic-trade/WMD-proliferation-financing violations; and specified tax crimes. Use the full current Sec. 3(i) text; list and numbering have been amended. (No verbatim: reviewer summarizes categories.)

AMLC = BSP Governor (chair) + IC Commissioner + SEC Chairman, acting unanimously. Functions: investigate suspicious/covered-deemed-suspicious transactions; institute forfeiture/remedial proceedings via OSG; cause prosecution complaints; investigate money laundering; seek search/seizure orders and subpoenas; implement targeted financial sanctions; manage frozen/forfeited assets.
provisions.verbatim: The Anti-Money Laundering Council is hereby created and shall be composed of the Governor of the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas as Chairman, the Commissioner of the Insurance Commission and the Chairman of the Securities and Exchange Commission, as members. The AMLC shall act unanimously in the discharge of its functions.

provisions.explanation: CA-issued freeze order on AMLC's verified ex parte petition upon probable cause: effective immediately for 20 days, summary hearing with notice, total cap 6 months. RTC asset-preservation orders in proper proceedings; deemed lifted if no case filed in time (pending-case rules apply); limited to the probable-cause amount; the account holder may move to lift. Ongpin: AMLC bears the burden of proving probable cause with a specific account-to-activity link.

sourceRefs.section: 8(a). Freezing of monetary instrument or property (Section 10)

provisions.verbatim: Upon a verified ex parte petition by the AMLC and after determination that probable cause exists that any monetary instrument or property is in any way related to an unlawful activity as defined in Section 3(i) hereof, the Court of Appeals may issue a freeze order which shall be effective immediately, for a period of twenty (20) days. Within the twenty (20)-day period, the Court of Appeals shall conduct a summary hearing, with notice to the parties, to determine whether or not to modify or lift the freeze order, or extend its effectivity. The total period of the freeze order issued by the Court of Appeals under this provision shall not exceed six (6) months.

provisions.explanation: AMLC may inquire into/examine particular deposits/investments with banks/NBFIs notwithstanding bank-secrecy laws, through required judicial authorization and procedures, with exceptions for specified predicates/related accounts. A bank inquiry examines records; it is not a seizure. Eugenio upholds the ex parte process because advance notice could frustrate investigation.

sourceRefs.section: 8(b). Authority to inquire into bank deposits (Section 11)

provisions.verbatim: Notwithstanding the provisions of Republic Act No. 1405, as amended; Republic Act No. 6426, as amended; Republic Act No. 8791; and other laws, the AMLC may inquire into or examine any particular deposit or investment with any banking institution or non-bank financial institution

provisions.explanation: AMLC may execute or refuse (with stated reason) foreign-State assistance requests under mutuality/reciprocity; may track, freeze, restrain, seize assets, share information, and seek forfeiture; and may request foreign assistance for tracing/preservation/information. Subject to authentication, treaty, statutory, and constitutional limits.

sourceRefs.section: 8(c). Request for assistance from foreign states (Section 13)

provisions.verbatim: Where a foreign State makes a request for assistance in the investigation or prosecution of a money laundering offense, the AMLC may execute the request or refuse to execute the same and inform the foreign State of any valid reason for not executing the request or for delaying the execution thereof. The principles of mutuality and reciprocity shall, for this purpose, be at all times recognized.

provisions.explanation: Good-faith CTR/STR reporting in regular duty performance immunizes the reporter from administrative, civil, or criminal proceedings even absent prosecution. Protection covers good-faith reporting only. Citation note: syllabus cites Rule 22, Sec. 7, but the amended IRR numbers safe harbor as Sec. 6 and confidentiality of reporting as Sec. 7.

sourceRefs.section: 9. Safe Harbor Provision (2018 AMLA IRR, Rule 22)

provisions.verbatim: No administrative, criminal or civil proceedings shall lie against any person for having made a CTR or an STR in the regular performance of his duties and in good faith, whether or not such reporting results in any criminal prosecution under the AMLA or any other Philippine law.

provisions.explanation: Tiered penalties: Sec. 4(a)-(d) = 7-14 years + ≥₱3M to ≤2x value; Sec. 4(e)-(f) = 4-7 years + ₱1.5M-₱3M; last paragraph of Sec. 4 = 6 months-4 years or ₱100k-₱500k or both. Other violations (record failures, malicious reporting, confidentiality breach, knowing participation, corporate officers) and administrative sanctions separately addressed. Check the consolidated law and later amendments before applying; mind non-retroactivity.
provisions.verbatim: The penalty of imprisonment ranging from seven (7) to fourteen (14) years and a fine of not less than Three million Philippine pesos (₱3,000,000.00) but not more than twice the value of the monetary instrument or property involved in the offense, shall be imposed upon a person convicted under Section 4(a), (b), (c) and (d) of this Act. The penalty of imprisonment from four (4) to seven (7) years and a fine of not less than One million five hundred thousand pesos (₱1,500,000.00) but not more than Three million pesos (₱3,000,000.00), shall be imposed upon a person convicted under Section 4(e) and (f) of this Act. The penalty of imprisonment from six (6) months to four (4) years or a fine of not less than One hundred thousand pesos (₱100,000.00) but not more than Five hundred thousand pesos (₱500,000.00), or both, shall be imposed on a person convicted under the last paragraph of Section 4 of this Act.

provisions.explanation: Institutional definitions: AMLC (RA 9160 council), ATC (RA 9372 council), and covered institutions (same meaning as under the AMLA as amended). RA 10168 works with the AMLA's reporting/investigation/freezing/forfeiture machinery.
provisions.verbatim: (a) Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) refers to the Council created by virtue of Republic Act No. 9160, as amended, otherwise known as the ‘Anti-Money Laundering Act of 2001, as amended’. (b) Anti-Terrorism Council (ATC) refers to the Council created by virtue of Republic Act No. 9372, otherwise known as the ‘Human Security Act of 2007’. (c) Covered institutions refer to or shall have the same meaning as defined under the Anti-Money Laundering Act (AMLA), as amended.

provisions.explanation: Dealing covers receipt, acquisition, transacting, representing, concealing, disposing/converting, transferring/moving, use as security, and providing financial services. Designated persons span UN-designated terrorists/financiers/organizations, Human Security Act-proscribed groups, and persons whose property is seizable under that Act on probable cause.

sourceRefs.section: 11(a). Terrorism financing and related definitions (RA 10168, Sections 3(d)–(e), (h)–(j), Sections 4–9 and 19)

provisions.verbatim: (d) Dealing, with regard to property or funds refers to receipt, acquisition, transacting, representing, concealing, disposing or converting, transferring or moving, use as security of or providing financial services. (e) Designated persons refers to: (1) any person or entity designated and/or identified as a terrorist, one who finances terrorism, or a terrorist organization or group under the applicable United Nations Security Council Resolution or by another jurisdiction or supranational jurisdiction; (2) any organization, association, or group of persons proscribed pursuant to Section 17 of the Human Security Act of 2007; or (3) any person, organization, association, or group of persons whose funds or property, based on probable cause, are subject to seizure and sequestration under Section 39 of the Human Security Act of 2007.

provisions.explanation: Property or funds span all financial assets/property plus title documents in any form (bank credits, cheques, money orders, shares, securities, bonds, drafts, letters of credit, accruing income/value). Terrorist = natural person committing/attempting/conspiring/participating/organizing/contributing to terrorist acts. Terrorist acts include statutory and treaty offenses, including civilian-targeted intimidation/compulsion violence. (Reviewer presents term names with gloss rather than a continuous quotation; no verbatim field.)

sourceRefs.section: 11(a). Terrorism financing and related definitions (RA 10168, Sections 3(d)–(e), (h)–(j), Sections 4–9 and 19)

provisions.explanation: Financing of terrorism: direct/indirect, willful, unexcused provision/collection/possession/use of property/funds/services with unlawful willful intent or knowledge they will support a terrorist act, organization, or individual terrorist. Intent/knowledge may be proved directly or inferred; actual use of the funds is not required.

sourceRefs.section: 11(a). Terrorism financing and related definitions (RA 10168, Sections 3(d)–(e), (h)–(j), Sections 4–9 and 19)

provisions.verbatim: Any person who, directly or indirectly, willfully and without lawful excuse, possesses, provides, collects or uses property or funds or makes available property, funds or financial service or other related services, by any means, with the unlawful and willful intention that they should be used or with the knowledge that they are to be used, in full or in part: (a) to carry out or facilitate the commission of any terrorist act; (b) by a terrorist organization, association or group; or (c) by an individual terrorist, shall be guilty of the crime of financing of terrorism.

provisions.explanation: Sec. 5: attempt/conspiracy and dealings with designated persons' property. Sec. 6: accomplices cooperating by previous/simultaneous acts. Sec. 7: accessories profiting/concealing/assisting escape. Sec. 8: dealing with or funding designated persons' property. Sec. 9: responsible officers of juridical persons; alien deportation. provisions.explanation: AMLC (own initiative or ATC request) investigates terrorism-financing-related property/funds and probable-cause persons, enlists government assistance, and may examine deposits/investments without a court order notwithstanding bank-secrecy laws for this section.
provisions.verbatim: The AMLC, either upon its own initiative or at the request of the ATC, is hereby authorized to investigate: (a) any property or funds that are in any way related to financing of terrorism or acts of terrorism; (b) property or funds of any person or persons in relation to whom there is probable cause to believe that such person or persons are committing or attempting or conspiring to commit, or participating in or facilitating the financing of terrorism or acts of terrorism as defined herein.

provisions.explanation: AMLC (own initiative or ATC request) issues ex parte freeze-without-delay orders over related property/funds or probable-cause persons/groups/organizations, with CA extensions; targeted-sanctions freezes last until the designation basis lifts. Distinct from the AMLA Sec. 10 track where the CA issues the freeze order.
provisions.verbatim: The AMLC, either upon its own initiative or at the request of the ATC, is hereby authorized to issue an ex parte order to freeze without delay: (a) property or funds that are in any way related to financing of terrorism or acts of terrorism; or (b) property or funds of any person, group of persons, terrorist organization, or association, in relation to whom there is probable cause to believe that they are committing or attempting or conspiring to commit, or participating in or facilitating the commission of financing of terrorism or acts of terrorism as defined herein.

provisions.explanation: Sec. 12: deferral of freeze orders for investigative/prosecutorial need. Sec. 13: humanitarian withdrawals for family sustenance, counsel, and medical needs per the specified decision-maker. Sec. 19: extra-territorial reach (outward-planned/inward-directed crimes, Philippine vessels/aircraft, diplomatic premises, Filipino victims, crimes against the government; Filipino nationals abroad). Three elements of the first paragraph: issuance to apply on account or for value; knowledge of insufficient funds/credit at issuance; subsequent dishonor (including unjustified stop-payment cases). Second paragraph: failing to keep funds/credit for 90-day presentment. Corporate checks: actual signatories liable. Penalties: 30 days-1 year, fine up to double the check capped at ₱200,000, or both. Constitutional: punishes issuance of worthless checks (police power), not debt non-payment (Lozano).

sourceRefs.section: 2(a). Issuance for value — Idos v. Court of Appeals

provisions.verbatim:
SEC. 1. Checks without sufficient funds.—Any person who makes or draws and issues any check to apply on account or for value, knowing at the time of issue that he does not have sufficient funds in or credit with the drawee bank for the payment of such check in full upon its presentment, which check is subsequently dishonored by the drawee bank for insufficiency of funds or credit or would have been dishonored for the same reason had not the drawer, without any valid reason, ordered the bank to stop payment, shall be punished by imprisonment of not less than thirty days but not more than one (1) year or by a fine of not less than but not more than double the amount of the check which fine shall in no case exceed Two Hundred Thousand Pesos, or both such fine and imprisonment at the discretion of the court.

The same penalty shall be imposed upon any person who, having sufficient funds in or credit with the drawee bank when he makes or draws and issues a check, shall fail to keep sufficient funds or to maintain a credit to cover the full amount of the check if presented within a period of ninety (90) days from the date appearing thereon, for which reason it is dishonored by the drawee bank.

Where the check is drawn by a corporation, company or entity, the person or persons who actually signed the check in behalf of such drawer shall be liable under this Act.

provisions.explanation: Rebuttable prima facie presumption of knowledge when a check presented within 90 days is dishonored and the drawer, after notice of nonpayment, fails to pay or arrange full payment within 5 banking days. Dishonor alone never conclusively proves knowledge; actual receipt of written notice matters (Lim Lao; Cabrera).

sourceRefs.section: 2(b). Knowledge of insufficiency of funds — Sections 1, 2 and 4; Lim Lao v. Court of Appeals

provisions.verbatim: SEC. 2. Evidence of knowledge of insufficient funds.—The making, drawing and issuance of a check payment of which is refused by the drawee because of insufficient funds in or credit with such bank, when presented within ninety (90) days from the date of the check, shall be prima facie evidence of knowledge of such insufficiency of funds or credit unless such maker or drawer pays the holder thereof the amount due thereon, or makes arrangements for payment in full by the drawee of such check within five (5) banking days after receiving notice that such check has not been paid by the drawee.

provisions.explanation: Credit means an arrangement or understanding with the drawee bank for payment — not a general third-party promise to pay.

sourceRefs.section: 2(b). Knowledge of insufficiency of funds — Sections 1, 2 and 4; Lim Lao v. Court of Appeals

provisions.verbatim: SEC. 4. Credit construed.—The word “credit” as used herein shall be construed to mean an arrangement or understanding with the bank for the payment of such check.

provisions.explanation: The drawee must note the dishonor reason on or attached to the check (always explicitly stating insufficient funds/credit when that is the fact, even after a stop-payment order). The dishonored check with the notation is prima facie evidence of issuance, presentment, dishonor, and proper dishonor for the stated reason — but does not prove knowledge. Sec. 3 (bank notation) is distinct from Sec. 2 (notice to drawer + 5-day opportunity).
provisions.verbatim:
SEC. 3. Duty of drawee; rules of evidence.—It shall be the duty of the drawee of any check, when refusing to pay the same to the holder thereof upon presentment, to cause to be written, printed, or stamped in plain language thereon, or attached thereto, the reason for drawee’s dishonor or refusal to pay the same: Provided, That where there are no sufficient funds in or credit with such drawee bank, such fact shall always be explicitly stated in the notice of dishonor or refusal. In all prosecutions under this Act, the introduction in evidence of any unpaid and dishonored check, having the drawee’s refusal to pay stamped or written thereon, or attached thereto, with the reason therefor as aforesaid, shall be prima facie evidence of the making or issuance of said check, and the due presentment to the drawee for payment and the dishonor thereof, and that the same was properly dishonored for the reason written, stamped or attached by the drawee on such dishonored check.

Notwithstanding receipt of an order to stop payment, the drawee shall state in the notice that there were no sufficient funds in or credit with such bank for the payment in full of such check, if such be the fact.

provisions.explanation: BP 22 prosecution is without prejudice to Revised Penal Code liability: the same check may support both a BP 22 and an estafa prosecution when each offense's distinct elements are proved (Nierras).
provisions.verbatim: SEC. 5. Liability under the Revised Penal Code.—Prosecution under this Act shall be without prejudice to any liability for violation of any provision of the Revised Penal Code.

provisions.citation: RPC Art. 315(2), as amended by RA 10951, Sec. 85
provisions.explanation: Estafa by false pretenses/fraudulent acts, including Art. 315(2)(d): postdating a check or issuing one in payment without sufficient funds. Failure to fund within 3 days from notice of dishonor is prima facie evidence of deceit. Deceit + damage distinguish estafa from BP 22; the 3-day deceit period differs from BP 22's 5-banking-day period. Tiered penalties keyed to the fraud amount (prisión mayor minimum up to reclusion perpetua). Quotation limited to Art. 315(2), the false-pretenses forms, and the 2(d) penalty schedule.

sourceRefs.section: 3(a). In relation to estafa — Revised Penal Code, Article 315(2); Nierras v. Dacuycuy

provisions.verbatim:
ART. 315. Swindling (estafa).—Any person who shall defraud another by any of the means mentioned hereinbelow shall be punished by:

2. By means of any of the following false pretenses or fraudulent acts executed prior to or simultaneously with the commission of the fraud:

(a) By using fictitious name, or falsely pretending to possess power, influence, qualifications, property, credit, agency, business or imaginary transactions, or by means of other similar deceits.

(b) By altering the quality, fineness or weight of anything pertaining to his art or business.

(c) By pretending to have bribed any Government employee, without prejudice to the action for calumny which the offended party may deem proper to bring against the offender. In this case, the offender shall be punished by the maximum period of the penalty.

(d) By postdating a check, or issuing a check in payment of an obligation when the offender had no funds in the bank, or his funds deposited therein were not sufficient to cover the amount of the check. The failure of the drawer of the check to deposit the amount necessary to cover his check within three (3) days from receipt of notice from the bank and/or the payee or holder that said check has been dishonored for lack or insufficiency of funds shall be prima facie evidence of deceit constituting false pretense or fraudulent act.

Any person who shall defraud another by means of false pretenses or fraudulent acts as defined in paragraph 2(d) hereof shall be punished by: (1) the penalty of reclusion temporal in its maximum period, if the amount of fraud is over Four million four hundred thousand pesos (₱4,400,000) but does not exceed Eight million eight hundred thousand pesos (₱8,800,000); if the amount exceeds the latter, the penalty shall be reclusion perpetua; (2) the penalty of reclusion temporal in its minimum and medium periods, if the amount of fraud is over Two million four hundred thousand pesos (₱2,400,000) but does not exceed Four million four hundred thousand pesos (₱4,400,000); (3) the penalty of prisión mayor in its maximum period, if the amount of fraud is over One million two hundred thousand pesos (₱1,200,000) but does not exceed Two million four hundred thousand pesos (₱2,400,000); (4) the penalty of prisión mayor in its medium period, if such amount is over Forty thousand pesos (₱40,000) but does not exceed One million two hundred thousand pesos (₱1,200,000); and (5) prisión mayor in its minimum period, if such amount does not exceed Forty thousand pesos (₱40,000).
